reason: Jacob (Israel), the patriarch and primary leader of the Hebrew family, demonstrates passivity and emotional grief rather than active accountability for the state of his people. When confronted with losses—Joseph's disappearance and Simeon's detention in Egypt—Jacob expresses personal sorrow ('עָלַי הָיוּ כֻלָּנָה'—'upon me are all these') but does not take proactive responsibility for resolving the people's circumstances. Instead, he reluctantly permits his sons to return to Egypt and accepts the unfolding of events with resignation. While his son Judah and the brothers eventually take accountability for their past actions toward Joseph ('אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים אֲנַחְנוּ'—'we are guilty'), Jacob as the overarching leader is characterized more by reactive grief and hesitation than by shouldering responsibility for improving the state of the Hebrew household during this crisis.
